Contracted divisors and Degree-Two MapsThanks: The work was supported by the Foundation for the Advancement of Theoretical Physics and Mathematics “BASIS”

Anton Trushin Email address: Trushin.ant.nic@yandex.ru Address: Faculty of Computer Science, HSE University, Pokrovsky Boulevard 11, Moscow, 109028 Russia
Abstract.

We consider polynomial maps of affine space over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. We prove that every irreducible component of the zero locus of the Jacobian determinant corresponds to either a contracted divisor or a branching divisor. We further consider polynomial maps of degree two without contracted divisors and show that the Jacobian determinant is irreducible, anti-invariant under the Galois involution, and coincides with the defining equation of the unique branching divisor.

1. Introduction

Let 𝕂\mathbb{K} be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and let 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} denote the affine space over 𝕂\mathbb{K}. Consider a polynomial map

φ:𝔸n→𝔸n,φ=f¯=(f1,…,fn),fi∈𝕂⁡[x¯],\varphi:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n},\qquad\varphi=\overline{f}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}),\quad f_{i}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}],

where x¯=(x1,…,xn)\overline{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}).

Let

J⁡(φ)=(∂fi∂xj)J(\varphi)=\left(\frac{\partial f_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}\right)

be the Jacobian matrix and write |J⁡(φ)|=detJ⁡(φ)\left|J(\varphi)\right|=\det J(\varphi).

A polynomial map is called a Keller map if |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right| is a nonzero constant. The Jacobian Conjecture, posed in [8], asserts that every Keller map is an automorphism. Despite considerable effort, the conjecture remains open even in dimension two.

One approach to the Jacobian Conjecture is to study the behaviour of irreducible polynomials under the dual homomorphism

φ∗:𝕂⁡(f¯)→𝕂⁡(x¯),φ∗​(H)=H⁡(f¯).\varphi^{*}:\mathbb{K}(\overline{f})\to\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}),\qquad\varphi^{*}(H)=H(\overline{f}).

By [1, Theorem 3.7], a Keller map φ:ℂn→ℂn\varphi:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} is invertible if and only if φ∗\varphi^{*} maps irreducible polynomials to irreducible ones. By [7, Theorem 5.1], this extends to arbitrary fields of characteristic zero: a polynomial map is invertible if and only if φ∗\varphi^{*} preserves irreducibility. Moreover, by [7, Theorem 5.2], for a Keller map the dual homomorphism φ∗\varphi^{*} sends square-free polynomials to square-free polynomials.

In Section 3 we introduce two types of divisors naturally associated with polynomial maps of affine space: contracted divisors, viewed as analogues of exceptional divisors of birational morphisms, and branching divisors, analogous to branch loci of finite morphisms. In Theorem 3.3.2 we show that every irreducible component of the zero locus of |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right| corresponds to either a contracted divisor or a branching divisor.

This dichotomy is natural, but we are not aware of a reference where it is stated explicitly, so we include a proof. As an application, we obtain an alternative proof of the result on square-free polynomials mentioned above.

We then consider polynomial maps of finite degree. Recall that the degree of φ\varphi is defined as the degree of the field extension 𝕂⁡(x¯)/𝕂⁡(f¯)\mathbb{K}(\overline{x})/\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}). By [2], the Jacobian Conjecture holds whenever this extension is Galois. In particular, this applies to maps of degree two. Further results for low degrees in dimension two were obtained in [9, 5, 4].

In Section 4 we study polynomial maps of degree two. In this case the field extension 𝕂⁡(x¯)/𝕂⁡(f¯)\mathbb{K}(\overline{x})/\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}) is Galois of degree two, and hence

Gal⁡(𝕂⁡(x¯),𝕂⁡(f¯))={i​d,τ},\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}),\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}))=\{id,\tau\},

where τ\tau is a birational involution.

We relate the action of τ\tau on 𝕂⁡(x¯)\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}) to the geometry of the fiber product

Z=𝔸n×φ𝔸n,Z=\mathbb{A}^{n}\times_{\varphi}\mathbb{A}^{n},

which parametrizes pairs of points with the same image under φ\varphi. For maps of degree two, the variety ZZ contains the graph of the involution τ\tau, while its remaining components correspond to subvarieties contracted by φ\varphi.

Using this description, we show that, in the absence of contracted divisors, the branching is governed by a single irreducible polynomial ss satisfying τ⁡(s)=−s\tau(s)=-s. In particular, all irreducible divisors of the Jacobian coincide with this polynomial, and we prove in Theorem 4.3.3 that

|J⁡(φ)|=s.\left|J(\varphi)\right|=s.

Thus, in this setting, the Jacobian is anti-invariant under the nontrivial Galois involution.

The author is grateful to Alexander Perepechko and Dmitry Trushin for numerous useful discussions and remarks.

2. Preliminaries, notation and conventions

Let 𝕂\mathbb{K} be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and let

φ:𝔸n→𝔸n,φ=(f¯)=(f1,…,fn),fj∈𝕂⁡[x¯],\varphi:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n},\qquad\varphi=(\overline{f})=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}),\quad f_{j}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}],

where x¯=(x1,…,xn)\overline{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}), be a polynomial map. We denote by

φ∗:𝕂⁡[f¯]→𝕂⁡[x¯],φ∗​(H)=H⁡(f¯),\varphi^{*}:\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}]\to\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}],\qquad\varphi^{*}(H)=H(\overline{f}),

the induced homomorphism of coordinate rings.

More generally, for a homomorphism of function fields

α:𝕂⁡(X)→𝕂⁡(Y)\alpha:\mathbb{K}(X)\to\mathbb{K}(Y)

we denote by

α∗:X⇢Y\alpha^{*}:X\dasharrow Y

the corresponding rational map.

Recall that the differential d​φd\varphi is the map of tangent spaces induced by the Jacobian matrix

J⁡(φ)=(∂fi∂xj)=(∂f¯∂x¯).J(\varphi)=\left(\frac{\partial f_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}\right)=\left(\frac{\partial\overline{f}}{\partial\overline{x}}\right).

For a variety XX we denote its tangent space by TXT_{X}, and by Ta,XT_{a,X} the tangent space at a point a∈Xa\in X. We say that d​φd\varphi is degenerate at a∈Xa\in X if

dim(da​φ​(Ta,X))<dimX.\dim\bigl(d_{a}\varphi(T_{a,X})\bigr)<\dim X.

We use the notation

∂H⁡(f¯)∂x¯=(∂H⁡(f1,…,fn)∂x1,…,∂H⁡(f1,…,fn)∂xn).\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{x}}=\left(\frac{\partial H(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n})}{\partial x_{1}},\ldots,\frac{\partial H(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n})}{\partial x_{n}}\right).

For a variety YY we denote by I⁡(Y)I(Y) its vanishing ideal, and for polynomials h1,…,hmh_{1},\ldots,h_{m} we write

𝕍⁡(h1,…,hm)\mathbb{V}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{m})

for their common zero locus.

By a general point of a variety XX we mean a point belonging to a Zariski open dense subset of XX.

We define the degree of φ\varphi as

degφ=[𝕂(x¯):𝕂(f¯)].\deg\varphi=[\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}):\mathbb{K}(\overline{f})].

Let XX be an irreducible variety and let

ξ:X⇢Y\xi:X\dasharrow Y

be a rational map. We define the graph Γξ\Gamma_{\xi} as the closure in X×YX\times Y of {(x,ξ⁡(x))∣x∈U}\{(x,\xi(x))\mid x\in U\}, where U⊂XU\subset X is any nonempty open subset on which ξ\xi is regular.

We now recall several basic facts concerning subvarieties contracted by a polynomial map.

An irreducible variety X⊆𝔸nX\subseteq\mathbb{A}^{n} is said to be contracted by φ\varphi, or simply contracted when φ\varphi is clear from the context, if

dimX>dimφ⁡(X).\dim X>\dim\varphi(X).

A reducible variety is contracted if each of its irreducible components is contracted.

If a variety XX is contracted, then the differential d​φd\varphi is degenerate at smooth points of XX, and the Jacobian |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right| vanishes on XX. Indeed, if Y=φ⁡(X)¯Y=\overline{\varphi(X)} and dimY<dimX\dim Y<\dim X, then for a general point a∈Xa\in X one has

dim(da​φ​(Ta​X))≤dimY<dimX,\dim\bigl(d_{a}\varphi(T_{a}X)\bigr)\leq\dim Y<\dim X,

which implies that the Jacobian matrix is singular along XX. In particular, if X=𝕍⁡(h)X=\mathbb{V}(h) is an irreducible hypersurface contracted by φ\varphi, then |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right| is divisible by hh.

The converse implication follows from a standard result (see [10, Chapter I, §5, Lemma 2.4]), which implies that if XX is irreducible and the differential d​φd\varphi is degenerate on a dense subset of XX, then dimφ⁡(X)<dimX\dim\varphi(X)<\dim X, and hence XX is contracted.

Proposition 2.0.1.

An irreducible variety XX is contracted by φ\varphi if and only if the differential d​φd\varphi is degenerate at a general point of XX.

Note that if φ\varphi is birational, then contracted divisors coincide with exceptional divisors (see [10]). However, in general, not every contraction is a contraction of a hypersurface.

Example 2.0.2.

Consider the map φ:𝔸3→𝔸3\varphi:\mathbb{A}^{3}\to\mathbb{A}^{3} given by

φ=(y​x2+z​x,y,z).\varphi=(yx^{2}+zx,y,z).

If (y,z)≠(0,0)(y,z)\neq(0,0), then a point has at most two preimages. Thus the only contracted subvariety is the line L={(x,0,0)}L=\{(x,0,0)\}.

We also recall the following standard result, often referred to as the Jacobian criterion. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    the map φ\varphi is dominant, equivalently, 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} is not contracted by φ\varphi;

  2. (2)

    the Jacobian determinant |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right| is not the zero polynomial;

  3. (3)

    the polynomials f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} are algebraically independent.

Moreover, if φ\varphi is dominant, then φ∗\varphi^{*} is injective and induces a finite field extension 𝕂⁡(f¯)⊂𝕂⁡(x¯).\mathbb{K}(\overline{f})\subset\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}).

We will also use the following standard fact (see [6, Proposition 7.16]): the number of preimages of a general point under a rational map ξ\xi is finite if and only if the induced homomorphism ξ∗\xi^{*} gives a finite extension of function fields 𝕂⁡(X)/𝕂⁡(Y)\mathbb{K}(X)/\mathbb{K}(Y); in this case, the number of preimages of a general point is equal to the degree of this extension.

3. Zeros of the Jacobian

3.1. Contractions and the dual map

We now study contracted divisors from the point of view of the dual map φ∗\varphi^{*}.

Proposition 3.1.1.

Let φ:𝔸n→𝔸n\varphi:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n} be a polynomial map without contracted divisors. Then the following statements hold.

  1. (1)

    If H1,H2∈𝕂⁡[f¯]H_{1},H_{2}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] are relatively prime, then H1​(f¯)H_{1}(\overline{f}) and H2​(f¯)H_{2}(\overline{f}) are relatively prime.

  2. (2)

    𝕂⁡[x¯]∩𝕂⁡(f¯)=𝕂⁡[f¯]\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]\cap\mathbb{K}(\overline{f})=\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}].

  3. (3)

    If h,g∈𝕂⁡[x¯]h,g\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}] are relatively prime and hg∈𝕂⁡(f¯)\frac{h}{g}\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}), then h,g∈𝕂⁡[f¯]h,g\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}].

Proof.

(1) Suppose that g=gcd⁡(H1​(f¯),H2​(f¯))g=\gcd(H_{1}(\overline{f}),H_{2}(\overline{f})) is nonconstant. Then

φ⁡(𝕍⁡(g))⊆𝕍⁡(H1)∩𝕍⁡(H2)=𝕍⁡(H1,H2).\varphi(\mathbb{V}(g))\subseteq\mathbb{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathbb{V}(H_{2})=\mathbb{V}(H_{1},H_{2}).

Since H1H_{1} and H2H_{2} are relatively prime, we have dim𝕍⁡(H1,H2)<n−1.\dim\mathbb{V}(H_{1},H_{2})<n-1. Hence

dimφ⁡(𝕍⁡(g))<n−1=dim𝕍⁡(g),\dim\varphi(\mathbb{V}(g))<n-1=\dim\mathbb{V}(g),

so 𝕍⁡(g)\mathbb{V}(g) is contracted, a contradiction.

(2) Let h=H1​(f¯)H2​(f¯)∈𝕂⁡[x¯]∩𝕂⁡(f¯),h=\frac{H_{1}(\overline{f})}{H_{2}(\overline{f})}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]\cap\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}), where H1H2\frac{H_{1}}{H_{2}} is reduced. By (1), the polynomials H1​(f¯)H_{1}(\overline{f}) and H2​(f¯)H_{2}(\overline{f}) are relatively prime. Since hh is a polynomial, the denominator must be constant, hence h∈𝕂⁡[f¯]h\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}].

(3) Write hg=H⁡(f¯)G⁡(f¯),\frac{h}{g}=\frac{H(\overline{f})}{G(\overline{f})}, where H,G∈𝕂⁡[f¯]H,G\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] and HG\frac{H}{G} is reduced. By (1), the polynomials H⁡(f¯)H(\overline{f}) and G⁡(f¯)G(\overline{f}) are relatively prime. Therefore the numerators and denominators of hg\frac{h}{g} and H⁡(f¯)G⁡(f¯)\frac{H(\overline{f})}{G(\overline{f})} differ only by a nonzero constant, hence h,g∈𝕂⁡[f¯]h,g\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}]. ∎

Proposition 3.1.2.

Let an irreducible hypersurface X=𝕍⁡(h)X=\mathbb{V}(h) be contracted by φ\varphi. Then there exist relatively prime irreducible polynomials H1,H2∈𝕂⁡[f¯]H_{1},H_{2}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] such that both φ∗​(H1)\varphi^{*}(H_{1}) and φ∗​(H2)\varphi^{*}(H_{2}) are divisible by hh.

Proof.

Let Y=φ⁡(X)¯Y=\overline{\varphi(X)}. Then YY is irreducible. Let I⁡(Y)I(Y) be generated by polynomials G1,…,GmG_{1},\ldots,G_{m}. Since YY is irreducible, we may assume that each GjG_{j} is irreducible. By assumption dimY<n−1\dim Y<n-1, hence among these generators there exist two relatively prime ones. ∎

To illustrate the phenomenon of contracted divisors, we give a simple example.

Example 3.1.3.

Let

φ:𝔸2→𝔸2,φ=(x​y,y)=(f1,f2).\varphi:\mathbb{A}^{2}\to\mathbb{A}^{2},\qquad\varphi=(xy,y)=(f_{1},f_{2}).

Then f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} are relatively prime in 𝕂⁡[f¯]\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}], but in 𝕂⁡[x¯]\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}] they have a common divisor:

gcd⁡(x​y,y)=y.\gcd(xy,y)=y.

In accordance with Proposition 3.1.1, the line

L={(x,0)}L=\{(x,0)\}

is contracted by φ\varphi, namely φ⁡(L)=(0,0)\varphi(L)=(0,0).

Note also that the fraction f1f2\frac{f_{1}}{f_{2}} is reduced in 𝕂⁡(f1,f2)\mathbb{K}(f_{1},f_{2}) but not reduced in 𝕂⁡(x,y)\mathbb{K}(x,y) (cf. 3.1.1), and

𝕂⁡[x,y]∩𝕂⁡(f1,f2)≠𝕂⁡[f1,f2],\mathbb{K}[x,y]\cap\mathbb{K}(f_{1},f_{2})\neq\mathbb{K}[f_{1},f_{2}],

since

f1f2=x∈𝕂⁡[x,y]∩𝕂⁡(f1,f2)\frac{f_{1}}{f_{2}}=x\in\mathbb{K}[x,y]\cap\mathbb{K}(f_{1},f_{2})

(cf. 3.1.1).

As an illustration of Proposition 3.1.1, consider h=xh=x, g=1g=1. They are relatively prime, and

x1=f1f2∈𝕂⁡(f¯),\frac{x}{1}=\frac{f_{1}}{f_{2}}\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}),

but h=x∉𝕂⁡[f¯]h=x\notin\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}].

3.2. Branching

We now describe the second type of special hypersurfaces, namely branching divisors. At the end of the section we show that the zero locus of the Jacobian consists of contractions and branchings.

Definition 3.1.

Let h∈𝕂⁡[x¯]h\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}] be irreducible. Let H∈𝕂⁡[f¯]H\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] be an irreducible polynomial such that H⁡(f¯)H(\overline{f}) is divisible by hh. Then HH is called an image polynomial of hh and is denoted by φ∗​(h)\varphi_{*}(h).

Proposition 3.2.1.

The image polynomial φ∗​(h)\varphi_{*}(h) exists for every irreducible hh. Moreover, if X=𝕍⁡(h)X=\mathbb{V}(h) is not contracted, then φ∗​(h)\varphi_{*}(h) is uniquely determined up to multiplication by a nonzero constant.

Proof.

The variety φ⁡(X)\varphi(X) is irreducible as the image of an irreducible variety. Hence φ∗​(h)\varphi_{*}(h) can be chosen as any irreducible polynomial in the ideal of φ⁡(X)¯\overline{\varphi(X)}.

Suppose now that XX is not contracted. Then dimφ⁡(X)=n−1\dim\varphi(X)=n-1, and therefore Y=φ⁡(X)¯Y=\overline{\varphi(X)} is an irreducible hypersurface. Hence Y=𝕍⁡(H)Y=\mathbb{V}(H) for some irreducible H∈𝕂⁡[f¯]H\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}], and this polynomial HH is unique up to a nonzero scalar multiple. ∎

Definition 3.2.

Let hh be irreducible and let X=𝕍⁡(h)X=\mathbb{V}(h) be not contracted by φ\varphi. Then XX is called a branching divisor for φ\varphi if φ∗​(φ∗​(h))\varphi^{*}(\varphi_{*}(h)) is divisible by h2h^{2}.

By Corollary 2.0.1, a variety XX is contracted by φ\varphi if and only if the differential d​φd\varphi is degenerate on the tangent space at a general point of XX. We now show that a non-contracted hypersurface X=𝕍⁡(h)X=\mathbb{V}(h) is a branching divisor if and only if the differential is degenerate on the conormal direction to φ⁡(X)\varphi(X).

Proposition 3.2.2.

Let h∈𝕂⁡[x¯]h\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}] be irreducible, let X=𝕍⁡(h)X=\mathbb{V}(h), and let H=φ∗​(h)H=\varphi_{*}(h). The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    XX is a branching divisor;

  2. (2)

    XX is not contracted and ∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)=0\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)=0 on XX.

Moreover, these conditions imply that |J⁡(φ)|=0\left|J(\varphi)\right|=0 on XX.

Proof.

Suppose first that XX is a branching divisor. Then H⁡(f¯)=h2​h0H(\overline{f})=h^{2}h_{0} for some h0∈𝕂⁡[x¯]h_{0}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]. By the chain rule,

∂H⁡(f¯)∂x¯=∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ).\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{x}}=\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi).

On the other hand,

∂H⁡(f¯)∂x¯=2​h​h0​∂h∂x¯+h2​∂h0∂x¯,\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{x}}=2hh_{0}\frac{\partial h}{\partial\overline{x}}+h^{2}\frac{\partial h_{0}}{\partial\overline{x}},

hence

∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)=h⁡(2​h0​∂h∂x¯+h​∂h0∂x¯),\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)=h\left(2h_{0}\frac{\partial h}{\partial\overline{x}}+h\frac{\partial h_{0}}{\partial\overline{x}}\right),

so the product vanishes on XX.

Since HH is irreducible, the vector ∂H∂f¯\frac{\partial H}{\partial\overline{f}} vanishes only on the singular locus of 𝕍⁡(H)\mathbb{V}(H), which has dimension at most n−2n-2. Since XX is not contracted, the image φ⁡(X)\varphi(X) is not contained in this singular locus. Hence ∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯≠0\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\neq 0 on a dense open subset of XX, and therefore ∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)=0\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)=0 implies that J⁡(φ)J(\varphi) is singular on a dense open subset of XX. Thus |J⁡(φ)|=0\left|J(\varphi)\right|=0 on XX.

Conversely, suppose that XX is not contracted and ∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)=0\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)=0 on XX. Write H⁡(f¯)=h​h0.H(\overline{f})=hh_{0}. Differentiating, we obtain

∂H⁡(f¯)∂x¯=∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)=h0​∂h∂x¯+h​∂h0∂x¯.\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{x}}=\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)=h_{0}\frac{\partial h}{\partial\overline{x}}+h\frac{\partial h_{0}}{\partial\overline{x}}.

Restricting to XX gives h0​∂h∂x¯=0.h_{0}\frac{\partial h}{\partial\overline{x}}=0. Since hh is irreducible, ∂h∂x¯\frac{\partial h}{\partial\overline{x}} does not vanish identically on XX. Hence hh divides h0h_{0}, and therefore H⁡(f¯)H(\overline{f}) is divisible by h2h^{2}. Thus XX is a branching divisor. ∎

3.3. Classification theorem

We now relate the behavior of the differential and its dual on the zero locus of the Jacobian.

Lemma 3.3.1.

Let hh be an irreducible divisor of |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right|, let X=𝕍⁡(h)X=\mathbb{V}(h), and let H=φ∗​(h)H=\varphi_{*}(h). Then for a point a∈Xr​e​ga\in X_{reg} at least one of the following holds:

  1. (1)

    ∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)=0\displaystyle\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)=0,

  2. (2)

    dim(da​φ​(Ta,X))≤n−2\displaystyle\dim\!\left(d_{a}\varphi(T_{a,X})\right)\leq n-2.

Proof.

Let T⁡(a)T(a) be a matrix whose columns form a basis of the tangent space Ta,XT_{a,X} at a point a∈Xr​e​ga\in X_{reg}. Then

rk⁡T⁡(a)=n−1,rk⁡(J⁡(φ)⋅T⁡(a))=dim(da​φ​(Ta,X)),\operatorname{rk}T(a)=n-1,\qquad\operatorname{rk}\!\left(J(\varphi)\cdot T(a)\right)=\dim\!\left(d_{a}\varphi(T_{a,X})\right),

and

∂h∂x¯⋅T⁡(a)=0.\frac{\partial h}{\partial\overline{x}}\cdot T(a)=0.

Let H⁡(f¯)=h​h0H(\overline{f})=hh_{0}. Differentiating gives

∂H⁡(f¯)∂x¯=∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)=h0​∂h∂x¯+h​∂h0∂x¯.\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{x}}=\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)=h_{0}\frac{\partial h}{\partial\overline{x}}+h\frac{\partial h_{0}}{\partial\overline{x}}.

Restricting to XX we obtain

∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)=h0​∂h∂x¯.\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)=h_{0}\frac{\partial h}{\partial\overline{x}}.

Multiplying on the right by T⁡(a)T(a) and using ∂h∂x¯⋅T⁡(a)=0\frac{\partial h}{\partial\overline{x}}\cdot T(a)=0, we get

∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)⋅T⁡(a)=0.\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)\cdot T(a)=0.

Applying Frobenius’ inequality to the product

∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)⋅T⁡(a),\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)\cdot T(a),

we obtain

rk⁡(∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ))+rk⁡(J⁡(φ)⋅T⁡(a))≤rk⁡(J⁡(φ)).\operatorname{rk}\!\left(\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)\right)+\operatorname{rk}\!\left(J(\varphi)\cdot T(a)\right)\leq\operatorname{rk}\!\left(J(\varphi)\right).

Since |J⁡(φ)|=0\left|J(\varphi)\right|=0 on XX, we have rk⁡J⁡(φ)≤n−1\operatorname{rk}J(\varphi)\leq n-1, and therefore

rk⁡(∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ))+rk⁡(J⁡(φ)⋅T⁡(a))≤n−1.\operatorname{rk}\!\left(\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)\right)+\operatorname{rk}\!\left(J(\varphi)\cdot T(a)\right)\leq n-1.

Hence, if

∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)≠0,\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)\neq 0,

then

rk⁡(J⁡(φ)⋅T⁡(a))≤n−2.\operatorname{rk}\!\left(J(\varphi)\cdot T(a)\right)\leq n-2.

∎

Theorem 3.3.2.

Every irreducible component of the zero locus of |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right| is either contracted by φ\varphi or is a branching divisor.

Proof.

Let hh be an irreducible divisor of |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right|, let X=𝕍⁡(h)X=\mathbb{V}(h), and let H=φ∗​(h)H=\varphi_{*}(h). Consider Xr​e​gX_{reg}.

By Lemma 3.3.1, for every point a∈Xr​e​ga\in X_{reg} one of the two conditions holds.

Since XX is irreducible, one of these conditions holds for a general point on XX.

If

∂H⁡(f¯)∂f¯⋅J⁡(φ)=0,\frac{\partial H(\overline{f})}{\partial\overline{f}}\cdot J(\varphi)=0,

then by Proposition 3.2.2, XX is a branching divisor.

If instead

dim(da​φ​(Ta,X))≤n−2\dim\!\left(d_{a}\varphi(T_{a,X})\right)\leq n-2

for a general point a∈Xa\in X, then by Corollary 2.0.1, XX is contracted. ∎

Note that if φ\varphi is finite, then by Theorem 3.3.2 points on a branching divisor are precisely branch points in the usual sense (see [10]). We now apply these results to Keller maps.

Proposition 3.3.3.

Let φ=(f¯)\varphi=(\overline{f}) and suppose |J⁡(φ)|∈𝕂×\left|J(\varphi)\right|\in\mathbb{K}^{\times}. Then

  1. (1)

    if H1,H2∈𝕂⁡[f¯]H_{1},H_{2}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] are coprime, then φ∗​(H1)\varphi_{*}(H_{1}) and φ∗​(H2)\varphi_{*}(H_{2}) are also coprime;

  2. (2)

    𝕂⁡[x¯]∩𝕂⁡(f¯)=𝕂⁡[f¯]\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]\cap\mathbb{K}(\overline{f})=\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}];

  3. (3)

    if an irreducible polynomial H∈𝕂⁡[f¯]H\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] is square-free, then φ∗​(H)\varphi^{*}(H) is also square-free.

Proof.

Since |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right| never vanishes, the map φ\varphi has no contracted divisors. Thus (1) and (2) follow from Proposition 3.1.1. Statement (3) follows from Proposition 3.2.2. ∎

As a corollary we obtain Keller’s theorem.

Corollary 3.3.4 (Keller’s theorem).

Let φ=(f¯)\varphi=(\overline{f}), |J⁡(φ)|∈𝕂×\left|J(\varphi)\right|\in\mathbb{K}^{\times}, and suppose 𝕂⁡(f¯)=𝕂⁡(x¯)\mathbb{K}(\overline{f})=\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}). Then φ\varphi is invertible.

Proof.

By Proposition 3.3.3(2) we have

𝕂⁡[f¯]=𝕂⁡[x¯]∩𝕂⁡(f¯)=𝕂⁡[x¯]∩𝕂⁡(x¯)=𝕂⁡[x¯],\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}]=\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]\cap\mathbb{K}(\overline{f})=\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]\cap\mathbb{K}(\overline{x})=\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}],

hence φ∗\varphi^{*} is an isomorphism. ∎

We now give an alternative proof of [3, Corollary 2.2].

Corollary 3.3.5.

The map φ\varphi is a Keller map if and only if the dual map φ∗\varphi^{*} sends square-free polynomials to square-free polynomials.

Proof.

Suppose |J⁡(φ)|∈𝕂×\left|J(\varphi)\right|\in\mathbb{K}^{\times} and let H∈𝕂⁡[f¯]H\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] be square-free. Write

H=H1⋯HmH=H_{1}\cdots H_{m}

as a product of irreducible polynomials.

By Proposition 3.3.3(3), each φ∗​(Hj)\varphi^{*}(H_{j}) is square-free, and by (1) the polynomials φ∗​(Hj)\varphi^{*}(H_{j}) and φ∗​(Hk)\varphi^{*}(H_{k}) are coprime for j≠kj\neq k.

Now suppose |J⁡(φ)|∉𝕂\left|J(\varphi)\right|\notin\mathbb{K}. Let hh be an irreducible divisor of |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right|. By Theorem 3.3.2, hh defines either a contraction or a branching divisor.

If hh defines a contraction, then by Proposition 3.1.2 there exist irreducible coprime polynomials H1,H2∈𝕂⁡[f¯]H_{1},H_{2}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] such that both φ∗​(H1)\varphi^{*}(H_{1}) and φ∗​(H2)\varphi^{*}(H_{2}) are divisible by hh. Hence φ∗​(H1​H2)\varphi^{*}(H_{1}H_{2}) is divisible by h2h^{2}.

If hh defines branching, then φ∗​(φ∗​(h))\varphi^{*}(\varphi_{*}(h)) is divisible by h2h^{2} by Definition 3.2. ∎

4. Degree-Two Maps

In this section we show that the Jacobian of a degree-two map without contracted divisors is an irreducible semi-invariant of the Galois involution.

4.1. Galois Involution and The Fiber Product

For a dominant polynomial map φ:𝔸n→𝔸n\varphi:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}, the field extension

𝕂⁡(f¯)⊂𝕂⁡(x¯)\mathbb{K}(\overline{f})\subset\mathbb{K}(\overline{x})

is finite, and its degree coincides with the number of points in a general fiber of φ\varphi.

Here we consider maps of degree two. In this case the extension 𝕂⁡(x¯)/𝕂⁡(f¯)\mathbb{K}(\overline{x})/\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}) is Galois, and the Galois group

Gal⁡(𝕂⁡(x¯),𝕂⁡(f¯))={i​d,τ}\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}),\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}))=\{id,\tau\}

consists of two elements, where τ\tau is a birational involution preserving 𝕂⁡(f¯)\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}). For the dual birational map we fix the notation θ=τ∗\theta=\tau^{*}.

We record the following observation.

Lemma 4.1.1.

If φ\varphi is a degree-two map, then for a general point a1a_{1} we have

φ−1​(φ⁡(a1))={a1,a2},θ⁡(a1)=a2.\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(a_{1}))=\{a_{1},a_{2}\},\qquad\theta(a_{1})=a_{2}.
Proof.

A general point has exactly two preimages, hence

φ−1​(φ⁡(a1))={a1,a2}.\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(a_{1}))=\{a_{1},a_{2}\}.

Since τ\tau preserves 𝕂⁡(f¯)\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}), we have τ⁡(f¯)=f¯\tau(\overline{f})=\overline{f}. Passing to the dual map θ\theta, we obtain φ∘θ=φ\varphi\circ\theta=\varphi. Substituting a1a_{1} gives

φ⁡(θ⁡(a1))=φ⁡(a1).\varphi(\theta(a_{1}))=\varphi(a_{1}).

Since τ≠i​d\tau\neq id, it follows that for a general point θ⁡(a1)\theta(a_{1}) is the second point in the fiber, hence

θ⁡(a1)=a2.\theta(a_{1})=a_{2}.

∎

Note that θ\theta being defined at a point aa does not imply, in general, that

φ−1​(φ⁡(a))={a,θ⁡(a)}.\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(a))=\{a,\theta(a)\}.
Example 4.1.2.

Let φ=(x​y,y2)\varphi=(xy,y^{2}). This map is the composition of the birational map (x​y,y)(xy,y) and the map (x,y2)(x,y^{2}), hence deg⁡φ=2\deg\varphi=2.

The map θ=(−x,−y)\theta=(-x,-y) preserves (x​y,y2)(xy,y^{2}) and is therefore the Galois involution. In this case θ\theta is defined on all points of 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}, while

φ−1​(φ⁡(1,0))={(x,0)}≠{(1,0),(−1,0)}.\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(1,0))=\{(x,0)\}\neq\{(1,0),(-1,0)\}.

Now let

Z=𝔸n×φ𝔸n⊂𝔸2​nZ=\mathbb{A}^{n}\times_{\varphi}\mathbb{A}^{n}\subset\mathbb{A}^{2n}

be the fiber product. It consists of pairs of points with the same image:

φ⁡(x¯1)=φ⁡(x¯2).\varphi(\overline{x}_{1})=\varphi(\overline{x}_{2}).

For a degree-two map we may consider the graph Γ=Γθ\varGamma=\varGamma_{\theta} of the map θ\theta, consisting of points of the form (a1,θ⁡(a1))(a_{1},\theta(a_{1})). By Lemma 4.1.1 we have

φ⁡(a1)=φ⁡(θ⁡(a1))=φ⁡(a2),\varphi(a_{1})=\varphi(\theta(a_{1}))=\varphi(a_{2}),

and therefore Γ⊂Z\varGamma\subset Z.

The variety ZZ also contains the diagonal Δ\Delta, consisting of points of the form (x¯,x¯)(\overline{x},\overline{x}). Note that ZZ is defined by nn equations in the 2​n2n-dimensional space 𝔸2​n\mathbb{A}^{2n}, hence every irreducible component of ZZ has dimension at least nn.

We now describe the tangent space TZT_{Z}. Consider the defining equations φ⁡(x¯1)=φ⁡(x¯2)\varphi(\overline{x}_{1})=\varphi(\overline{x}_{2}). Writing them as

fj​(x¯1)−fj​(x¯2)=0f_{j}(\overline{x}_{1})-f_{j}(\overline{x}_{2})=0

and taking partial derivatives we obtain

∂(fj​(x¯1)−fj​(x¯2))∂x1,k\displaystyle\frac{\partial(f_{j}(\overline{x}_{1})-f_{j}(\overline{x}_{2}))}{\partial x_{1,k}} =∂fj​(x¯1)∂x1,k,\displaystyle=\frac{\partial f_{j}(\overline{x}_{1})}{\partial x_{1,k}},
∂(fj​(x¯1)−fj​(x¯2))∂x2,k\displaystyle\frac{\partial(f_{j}(\overline{x}_{1})-f_{j}(\overline{x}_{2}))}{\partial x_{2,k}} =−∂fj​(x¯2)∂x2,k.\displaystyle=-\frac{\partial f_{j}(\overline{x}_{2})}{\partial x_{2,k}}.

Arranging these partial derivatives into rows, we obtain the normal matrix NN of size n×2​nn\times 2n:

N=(J​(φ)​(x¯1)−J​(φ)​(x¯2)).N=\begin{pmatrix}J(\varphi)(\overline{x}_{1})&-J(\varphi)(\overline{x}_{2})\end{pmatrix}.

For points (a1,a2)(a_{1},a_{2}) such that |J⁡(φ)|​(aj)≠0\left|J(\varphi)\right|(a_{j})\neq 0, the matrix NN has full rank, and hence the dimension of the tangent space at such points is at most nn.

Since both Γ\varGamma and Δ\Delta have dimension nn, they are irreducible components of ZZ. Let Z′Z^{\prime} denote the union of the remaining components. Then

Z=Δ∪Γ∪Z′.Z=\Delta\cup\varGamma\cup Z^{\prime}.

Consider the projections π1,π2\pi_{1},\pi_{2} given by

πj​(a1,a2)=aj.\pi_{j}(a_{1},a_{2})=a_{j}.
Proposition 4.1.3.

Let X=πj​(Z′)⊂𝔸nX=\pi_{j}(Z^{\prime})\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}. Then

  1. (1)

    dimX≤n−1\dim X\leq n-1;

  2. (2)

    XX is contracted by the map φ\varphi.

Proof.

(1) For a general point a∈𝔸na\in\mathbb{A}^{n}, its fiber π1−1​(a)\pi_{1}^{-1}(a) consists of points of the form (a,b)(a,b) such that b∈φ−1​(φ⁡(a))b\in\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(a)). Moreover, if a=ba=b then (a,b)∈Δ(a,b)\in\Delta, while if a≠ba\neq b then (a,b)∈Γ(a,b)\in\varGamma. Hence for a general point the fiber πj−1​(a)\pi_{j}^{-1}(a) contains no points of Z′Z^{\prime}, and therefore the dimension of X=πj​(Z′)X=\pi_{j}(Z^{\prime}) is at most n−1n-1.

(2) The dimension of Z′Z^{\prime} is at least nn, while dimX≤n−1\dim X\leq n-1. Hence for a point a∈Xa\in X the fiber π1−1​(a)\pi_{1}^{-1}(a) is at least one-dimensional. Let

Y=π2​(π1−1​(a)).Y=\pi_{2}(\pi_{1}^{-1}(a)).

Then YY is also at least one-dimensional and φ⁡(Y)=φ⁡(a)\varphi(Y)=\varphi(a). Since YY is contracted to a point, the differential d​φd\varphi is degenerate on the tangent space TYT_{Y} at general points. Since TY⊂TXT_{Y}\subset T_{X}, the differential is also degenerate on the tangent space to XX. Hence XX is contracted by φ\varphi by Corollary 2.0.1. ∎

Corollary 4.1.4.

If φ\varphi has no contracted divisors, then dimπj​(Z′)<n−1\dim\pi_{j}(Z^{\prime})<n-1.

Example 4.1.5.

Consider the map

φ:𝔸2→𝔸2,φ⁡(x,y)=(x​y,y2).\varphi:\mathbb{A}^{2}\to\mathbb{A}^{2},\qquad\varphi(x,y)=(xy,y^{2}).

This map is the composition of the birational isomorphism (x​y,y)(xy,y) and the degree-two map (x,y2)(x,y^{2}), hence deg⁡φ=2\deg\varphi=2.

The variety Z=𝔸2×φ𝔸2Z=\mathbb{A}^{2}\times_{\varphi}\mathbb{A}^{2} is defined by the equations

x1​y1\displaystyle x_{1}y_{1} =x2​y2,\displaystyle=x_{2}y_{2},
y12\displaystyle y_{1}^{2} =y22.\displaystyle=y_{2}^{2}.

Thus ZZ is the union of three two-dimensional components:

Z=Δ∪Γ∪Z′,Z=\Delta\cup\varGamma\cup Z^{\prime},

where

Δ=𝕍⁡(x1−x2,y1−y2),Γ=𝕍⁡(x1+x2,y1+y2),Z′=𝕍⁡(y1,y2).\Delta=\mathbb{V}(x_{1}-x_{2},y_{1}-y_{2}),\qquad\varGamma=\mathbb{V}(x_{1}+x_{2},y_{1}+y_{2}),\qquad Z^{\prime}=\mathbb{V}(y_{1},y_{2}).

Under the projection π1\pi_{1}, the component Z′Z^{\prime} maps to the line

L={(x,0)},L=\{(x,0)\},

which is contracted to the point (0,0)(0,0) by φ\varphi.

To illustrate Corollary 4.1.4 and the fact that the absence of contracted divisors does not imply the absence of the component Z′Z^{\prime}, we give another example.

Example 4.1.6.

Consider the map φ:𝔸4→𝔸4\varphi:\mathbb{A}^{4}\to\mathbb{A}^{4} defined by

φ​(xyzw)=(w​x2+z​yz​x+w​yzw).\varphi\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\\ z\\ w\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}wx^{2}+zy\\ zx+wy\\ z\\ w\end{pmatrix}.

We first show that this map has degree two. Consider the preimage of a point (x0,y0,z0,w0)(x_{0},y_{0},z_{0},w_{0}) with z0≠0z_{0}\neq 0 and w0≠0w_{0}\neq 0:

{w​x2+z​y=x0z​x+w​y=y0z=z0w=w0⟺{w​x2−z2w​x=x0−zw​y0z​x+w​y=y0z=z0w=w0\begin{cases}wx^{2}+zy=x_{0}\\ zx+wy=y_{0}\\ z=z_{0}\\ w=w_{0}\end{cases}\Longleftrightarrow\begin{cases}wx^{2}-\frac{z^{2}}{w}x=x_{0}-\frac{z}{w}y_{0}\\ zx+wy=y_{0}\\ z=z_{0}\\ w=w_{0}\end{cases}

The equation

w​x2−z2w​x−x0+zw​y0=0wx^{2}-\frac{z^{2}}{w}x-x_{0}+\frac{z}{w}y_{0}=0

is quadratic in xx and has two distinct roots provided its discriminant

D=z4w2−4​(z​y0−w​x0)D=\frac{z^{4}}{w^{2}}-4(zy_{0}-wx_{0})

is nonzero. Hence a general point has exactly two preimages. In particular, if (z0,w0)≠(0,0)(z_{0},w_{0})\neq(0,0) then the point has at most two preimages, and hence φ\varphi has no contracted divisors.

At the same time the two-dimensional plane 𝕍⁡(z,w)\mathbb{V}(z,w) is contracted to the point (0,0)(0,0).

The variety ZZ contains the two-dimensional component

Z′=𝕍⁡(z1,w1,z2,w2).Z^{\prime}=\mathbb{V}(z_{1},w_{1},z_{2},w_{2}).

Its image under π1\pi_{1} is the contracted plane 𝕍⁡(z,w)\mathbb{V}(z,w), which has dimension two.

4.2. Semi-invariants

We begin by constructing an element s∈𝕂⁡(x¯)s\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}) such that τ⁡(s)=−s\tau(s)=-s. For this, we take any h∈𝕂⁡(x¯)∖𝕂⁡(f¯)h\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{x})\setminus\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}) and set

s=h−τ⁡(h).s=h-\tau(h).
Lemma 4.2.1.

Let φ\varphi be a degree-two map. Then there exists s∈𝕂⁡[x¯]s\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}] such that τ⁡(s)=−s\tau(s)=-s and S⁡(f¯)=s2∈𝕂⁡[f¯]S(\overline{f})=s^{2}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] is square-free.

Proof.

Take a nonzero s~∈𝕂⁡(x¯)\widetilde{s}\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}) such that τ⁡(s~)=−s~\tau(\widetilde{s})=-\widetilde{s} and write S~​(f¯)=s~2\widetilde{S}(\overline{f})=\widetilde{s}^{2}.

Factor S~\widetilde{S} as

S~=S1⋯SmS02,\widetilde{S}=S_{1}\cdots S_{m}S_{0}^{2},

where S1,…,SmS_{1},\ldots,S_{m} are pairwise coprime irreducible polynomials and S0∈𝕂⁡(f¯)S_{0}\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}). Dividing s~\widetilde{s} by S0S_{0}, we obtain an element s=s~/S0s=\widetilde{s}/S_{0} such that s2s^{2} is square-free. ∎

Corollary 4.2.2.

For a degree-two map we have |J⁡(φ)|∉𝕂×\left|J(\varphi)\right|\notin\mathbb{K}^{\times}.

Proof.

Assume that φ\varphi has no contracted divisors. Let s0s_{0} be an irreducible divisor of Sj​(f¯)S_{j}(\overline{f}). Then φ∗​(s0)=Sj\varphi_{*}(s_{0})=S_{j}.

Since Sj​(f¯)S_{j}(\overline{f}) is a square in 𝕂⁡[x¯]\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}], it is divisible by s02s_{0}^{2}, so s0s_{0} defines a branching divisor. By Proposition 3.2.2, s0s_{0} divides |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right|. ∎

We now study how branching is reflected in the action of τ\tau on 𝕂⁡(x¯)\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}). From now on we assume that φ\varphi has no contracted divisors.

Lemma 4.2.3.

Let h∈𝕂⁡[x¯]h\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    τ⁡(h)=−h\tau(h)=-h;

  2. (2)

    h∉𝕂⁡[f¯]h\notin\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] and h2∈𝕂⁡[f¯]h^{2}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}];

  3. (3)

    h∉𝕂⁡(f¯)h\notin\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}) and there exists mm such that hm∈𝕂⁡(f¯)h^{m}\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}).

Proof.

If τ⁡(h)=−h\tau(h)=-h, then τ⁡(h)​h=−h2\tau(h)h=-h^{2} is invariant under τ\tau, hence h2∈𝕂⁡(f¯)h^{2}\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}), and therefore h2∈𝕂⁡[f¯]h^{2}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] by Proposition 3.1.1.

The implication (2)⇒(3)(2)\Rightarrow(3) is immediate with m=2m=2.

Finally, suppose hm∈𝕂⁡(f¯)h^{m}\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}). Writing τ⁡(h)=h^\tau(h)=\widehat{h}, we get hm=h^mh^{m}=\widehat{h}^{m}, so h=λ​h^h=\lambda\widehat{h} for some mm-th root of unity λ\lambda. Since τ\tau has order two, λ=±1\lambda=\pm 1. Since h∉𝕂⁡(f¯)h\notin\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}), we conclude λ=−1\lambda=-1. ∎

Lemma 4.2.4.

Let h∈𝕂⁡[x¯]∖𝕂⁡[f¯]h\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]\setminus\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] be irreducible and assume that h2∈𝕂⁡[f¯]h^{2}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}]. Then

φ∗​(φ∗​(h))=h2andτ⁡(h)=−h.\varphi^{*}(\varphi_{*}(h))=h^{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tau(h)=-h.
Proof.

Let H=φ∗​(φ∗​(h))H=\varphi^{*}(\varphi_{*}(h)). Then HH divides h2h^{2}. Since h∉𝕂⁡[f¯]h\notin\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}], we must have H=h2H=h^{2}. The relation τ⁡(h)=−h\tau(h)=-h follows from Lemma 4.2.3. ∎

We now view polynomials from 𝕂⁡[x¯]\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}] as functions on the variety Γ\varGamma via the projection π1\pi_{1}. Then θ\theta acts on Γ\varGamma by

θ⁡(a1,a2)=(a2,a1).\theta(a_{1},a_{2})=(a_{2},a_{1}).
Lemma 4.2.5.

Let g∈𝕂⁡[x¯]∩𝕂​[Γ]×g\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]\cap\mathbb{K}[\varGamma]^{\times} be irreducible. Then either g∈𝕂⁡[f¯]g\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] or τ⁡(g)=−g\tau(g)=-g.

Proof.

Let G=φ∗​(g)G=\varphi_{*}(g) and write G⁡(f¯)=g⋅g0G(\overline{f})=g\cdot g_{0}.

The images of 𝕍⁡(g)\mathbb{V}(g) and 𝕍⁡(g0)\mathbb{V}(g_{0}) both contain open subsets of 𝕍⁡(G)\mathbb{V}(G), since there are no contracted divisors. Hence for a general point a∈𝕍⁡(g)a\in\mathbb{V}(g) there exists a0∈𝕍⁡(g0)a_{0}\in\mathbb{V}(g_{0}) such that φ⁡(a)=φ⁡(a0)\varphi(a)=\varphi(a_{0}), so (a,a0)∈Z(a,a_{0})\in Z.

Since gg is invertible on Γ\varGamma, such points cannot lie on Γ\varGamma. Excluding the lower-dimensional part coming from Z′Z^{\prime}, we conclude that generically (a,a0)(a,a_{0}) lies on the diagonal. Therefore gg and g0g_{0} have the same irreducible divisors, and the claim follows from Lemma 4.2.3. ∎

Corollary 4.2.6.

Let g∈𝕂​[Γ]×g\in\mathbb{K}[\varGamma]^{\times}. Then either g∈𝕂⁡(f¯)g\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}) or τ⁡(g)=−g\tau(g)=-g.

Proof.

Write gg as a quotient of two polynomials and apply Lemma 4.2.5 to each irreducible factor. ∎

Lemma 4.2.7.

Let h∈𝕂⁡[x¯]h\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}] and suppose

τ⁡(h)=pr\tau(h)=\frac{p}{r}

is a reduced fraction. Then r∈𝕂⁡[f¯]r\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}].

Proof.

Consider the sum

h+τ⁡(h)=r​h+pr.h+\tau(h)=\frac{rh+p}{r}.

Let dd be an irreducible divisor of rr. Then dd does not divide pp, and therefore does not divide the numerator r​h+prh+p. Since h+τ⁡(h)∈𝕂⁡(f¯)h+\tau(h)\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}), it follows from Proposition 3.1.1 that r∈𝕂⁡[f¯]r\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}]. ∎

Lemma 4.2.8.

Let h1∈𝕂⁡[x¯]∖𝕂​[Γ]×h_{1}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]\setminus\mathbb{K}[\varGamma]^{\times} be irreducible. Then

τ⁡(h1)=g​h2,\tau(h_{1})=gh_{2},

where h2h_{2} is irreducible and noninvertible on Γ\varGamma, and g∈𝕂​[Γ]×∩𝕂⁡(f¯)g\in\mathbb{K}[\varGamma]^{\times}\cap\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}).

Proof.

The function h1h_{1} vanishes on Γ\varGamma but has no poles there, and the same holds for τ⁡(h1)\tau(h_{1}). Therefore all noninvertible factors of τ⁡(h1)\tau(h_{1}) must appear in the numerator.

Separating invertible and noninvertible factors, we obtain a decomposition of the required form. Irreducibility of h2h_{2} follows from applying τ\tau and comparing factors. That g∈𝕂⁡[f¯]g\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] follows from Lemma 4.2.7. ∎

Lemma 4.2.9.

Let h1∈𝕂⁡[x¯]∖𝕂​[Γ]×h_{1}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]\setminus\mathbb{K}[\varGamma]^{\times} be irreducible and assume h1∉𝕂⁡[f¯]h_{1}\notin\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}]. Then

φ∗​(φ∗​(h1))=h1​h2,\varphi^{*}(\varphi_{*}(h_{1}))=h_{1}h_{2},

where h2h_{2} is as in Lemma 4.2.8.

Proof.

Using Lemma 4.2.8, we write τ⁡(h1)=h2⋅g\tau(h_{1})=h_{2}\cdot g with gg invertible on Γ\varGamma. Applying τ\tau again shows that h1​h2h_{1}h_{2} is invariant, hence lies in 𝕂⁡[f¯]\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}].

The images of 𝕍⁡(h1)\mathbb{V}(h_{1}) and 𝕍⁡(h2)\mathbb{V}(h_{2}) coincide, so their common image is defined by some irreducible H∈𝕂⁡[f¯]H\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}]. Comparing multiplicities shows that φ∗​(H)=h1​h2\varphi^{*}(H)=h_{1}h_{2}. ∎

Lemma 4.2.10.

Let hh be an irreducible polynomial defining a branching divisor. Then

φ∗​(φ∗​(h))=h2andτ⁡(h)=−h.\varphi^{*}(\varphi_{*}(h))=h^{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tau(h)=-h.
Proof.

Since hh defines branching, it is not contained in 𝕂⁡[f¯]\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}]. If hh is invertible on Γ\varGamma, the statement follows from previous results on invertible elements.

Otherwise we apply Lemma 4.2.9. In this case branching forces h1=h2h_{1}=h_{2}, hence φ∗​(φ∗​(h))=h2\varphi^{*}(\varphi_{*}(h))=h^{2}. The relation τ⁡(h)=−h\tau(h)=-h follows from Lemma 4.2.3. ∎

Proposition 4.2.11.

Let φ\varphi be a degree-two map without contracted divisors. Then there exists an irreducible s∈𝕂⁡[x¯]s\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}] such that τ⁡(s)=−s\tau(s)=-s. Moreover, ss is unique up to multiplication by a constant.

Proof.

By Corollary 4.2.2, a branching divisor exists. Let ss be an irreducible polynomial defining it. Then τ⁡(s)=−s\tau(s)=-s by Lemma 4.2.10.

If s0s_{0} is another such polynomial, then τ⁡(s0/s)=s0/s\tau(s_{0}/s)=s_{0}/s, hence s0/s∈𝕂⁡(f¯)s_{0}/s\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}). By Proposition 3.1.1, s0/s∈𝕂⁡[f¯]s_{0}/s\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}], so s0=λ​ss_{0}=\lambda s. ∎

Corollary 4.2.12.

If φ\varphi has no contracted divisors, then the Jacobian |J⁡(φ)|\left|J(\varphi)\right| has a unique irreducible divisor ss.

Proof.

By Theorem 3.3.2, every irreducible divisor of the Jacobian defines branching. By Proposition 4.2.11, such a divisor is unique. ∎

4.3. Jacobian

By Corollary 4.2.12, if φ\varphi has degree-two and no contracted divisors, then

|J⁡(φ)|=sk\left|J(\varphi)\right|=s^{k}

for some irreducible ss such that τ⁡(s)=−s\tau(s)=-s and some integer k>0k>0. Fix such an ss, and set S=s2∈𝕂⁡(f¯)S=s^{2}\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}), which lies in 𝕂⁡[f¯]\mathbb{K}[\overline{f}] and is irreducible since φ\varphi has no contracted divisors.

Consider the polynomial

q=t2−S∈𝕂⁡[t,f1,…,fn]q=t^{2}-S\in\mathbb{K}[t,f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}]

and the hypersurface

M=𝕍⁡(q)⊂𝔸n+1.M=\mathbb{V}(q)\subset\mathbb{A}^{n+1}.

Then φ\varphi factors as φ=π∘ψ\varphi=\pi\circ\psi, where

ψ:𝔸n→M,ψ⁡(x¯)=(s⁡(x¯),φ⁡(x¯)),\psi:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to M,\qquad\psi(\overline{x})=(s(\overline{x}),\varphi(\overline{x})),

and π\pi is the projection

π⁡(t,f1,…,fn)=(f1,…,fn).\pi(t,f_{1},\ldots,f_{n})=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}).

For j=0,…,nj=0,\ldots,n, we define polynomial maps

φ0=φ,φj=(f1,…,fj−1,s,fj+1,…,fn)​for ​j≥1.\varphi_{0}=\varphi,\qquad\varphi_{j}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{j-1},s,f_{j+1},\ldots,f_{n})\ \text{for }j\geq 1.
Lemma 4.3.1.

At smooth points of MM the vectors

(sk,|J⁡(φ1)|,…,|J⁡(φn)|)(s^{k},|J(\varphi_{1})|,\ldots,|J(\varphi_{n})|)

and

(2​s,ψ∗​(∂q∂f1),…,ψ∗​(∂q∂fn))\left(2s,\psi^{*}\!\left(\frac{\partial q}{\partial f_{1}}\right),\ldots,\psi^{*}\!\left(\frac{\partial q}{\partial f_{n}}\right)\right)

are collinear.

Proof.

The hypersurface MM is defined by the equation q=t2−Sq=t^{2}-S, hence its normal vector at a smooth point is

(2​t,∂q∂f1,…,∂q∂fn).\left(2t,\frac{\partial q}{\partial f_{1}},\ldots,\frac{\partial q}{\partial f_{n}}\right).

Pulling back via ψ\psi, we obtain

(2​s,ψ∗​(∂q∂f1),…,ψ∗​(∂q∂fn)).\left(2s,\psi^{*}\!\left(\frac{\partial q}{\partial f_{1}}\right),\ldots,\psi^{*}\!\left(\frac{\partial q}{\partial f_{n}}\right)\right).

On the other hand, consider the Jacobian matrix

J⁡(ψ)=(∂s∂x1⋯∂s∂xn∂f1∂x1⋯∂f1∂xn⋱∂fn∂x1⋯∂fn∂xn).J(\psi)=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\partial s}{\partial x_{1}}&\cdots&\frac{\partial s}{\partial x_{n}}\\ \frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x_{1}}&\cdots&\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x_{n}}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \frac{\partial f_{n}}{\partial x_{1}}&\cdots&\frac{\partial f_{n}}{\partial x_{n}}\end{pmatrix}.

Its columns are tangent vectors to MM. Let (A1,…,An+1)(A_{1},\ldots,A_{n+1}) be the vector of signed maximal minors of J⁡(ψ)J(\psi). Then

(A1,…,An+1)⋅J⁡(ψ)=0,(A_{1},\ldots,A_{n+1})\cdot J(\psi)=0,

hence this vector is orthogonal to all tangent vectors and therefore defines a normal vector.

Moreover, by construction of the minors we have

A1=|J(φ0)|=|J(φ)|,Aj+1=|J(φj)|for j=1,…,n.A_{1}=|J(\varphi_{0})|=\left|J(\varphi)\right|,\qquad A_{j+1}=|J(\varphi_{j})|\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,n.

Since the normal space to a hypersurface at a smooth point is one-dimensional, the two normal vectors are collinear. ∎

Lemma 4.3.2.

If 𝕍⁡(s)\mathbb{V}(s) is not contracted, then

gcd⁡(|J⁡(φ0)|,|J⁡(φ1)|,…,|J⁡(φn)|)=1.\gcd(|J(\varphi_{0})|,|J(\varphi_{1})|,\ldots,|J(\varphi_{n})|)=1.
Proof.

For j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n, denote by

πj:𝔸n→𝔸n−1\pi_{j}:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n-1}

the projection forgetting the jj-th coordinate.

First note that for any j>0j>0 the polynomial ss lies in 𝕂⁡[f1,…,fj−1,s,fj+1,…,fn]\mathbb{K}[f_{1},\ldots,f_{j-1},s,f_{j+1},\ldots,f_{n}], hence ss does not define branching for φj\varphi_{j}. Let X=φ⁡(𝕍⁡(s))¯X=\overline{\varphi(\mathbb{V}(s))} and let a∈Xa\in X be a smooth point. The tangent space at aa is given by

α1​x1+…+αn​xn=0\alpha_{1}x_{1}+\ldots+\alpha_{n}x_{n}=0

with (α1,…,αn)≠0(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n})\neq 0. Choose αj≠0\alpha_{j}\neq 0. Then πj\pi_{j} does not contract XX by Proposition 2.0.1, hence φj\varphi_{j} does not contract XX.

Thus |J⁡(φj)||J(\varphi_{j})| is not divisible by ss by Theorem 3.3.2, while |J⁡(φ0)|=|J⁡(φ)||J(\varphi_{0})|=\left|J(\varphi)\right| is divisible only by ss by Corollary 4.2.12. ∎

Theorem 4.3.3.

Let φ:𝔸n→𝔸n\varphi:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}, φ=(f¯)\varphi=(\overline{f}) be a degree-two map without contracted divisors and suppose

Gal⁡(𝕂⁡(x¯),𝕂⁡(f¯))={i​d,τ}.\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}),\mathbb{K}(\overline{f}))=\{id,\tau\}.

Then

|J⁡(φ)|=s,\left|J(\varphi)\right|=s,

where ss is irreducible and τ⁡(s)=−s\tau(s)=-s.

Proof.

By Lemma 4.3.1, there exist λ1,λ2∈𝕂⁡(x¯)\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\in\mathbb{K}(\overline{x}) such that

λ1​(sk,|J⁡(φ1)|,…,|J⁡(φn)|)=λ2​(2​s,ψ∗​(∂q∂f1),…,ψ∗​(∂q∂fn)).\lambda_{1}(s^{k},|J(\varphi_{1})|,\ldots,|J(\varphi_{n})|)=\lambda_{2}\left(2s,\psi^{*}\!\left(\frac{\partial q}{\partial f_{1}}\right),\ldots,\psi^{*}\!\left(\frac{\partial q}{\partial f_{n}}\right)\right).

Multiplying both sides by a common denominator, we may assume that λ1,λ2∈𝕂⁡[x¯]\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\in\mathbb{K}[\overline{x}]. Dividing by their greatest common divisor, we may further assume that they are coprime. By Lemma 4.3.2, gcd⁡(|J⁡(φ0)|,…,|J⁡(φn)|)=1\gcd(|J(\varphi_{0})|,\ldots,|J(\varphi_{n})|)=1, so λ2∈𝕂×\lambda_{2}\in\mathbb{K}^{\times}. Comparing the first coordinates, we obtain

λ1​sk=2​λ2​s.\lambda_{1}s^{k}=2\lambda_{2}s.

Hence λ1∈𝕂×\lambda_{1}\in\mathbb{K}^{\times} and k=1k=1.

∎

Example 4.3.4.

As an application of Theorem 4.3.3, we compute the Galois involution for the map from Example 4.1.6:

φ​(xyzw)=(w​x2+z​yz​x+w​yzw).\varphi\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\\ z\\ w\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}wx^{2}+zy\\ zx+wy\\ z\\ w\end{pmatrix}.

We have already shown that this map has degree two and has no contracted divisors. Hence Theorem 4.3.3 applies, and the Jacobian determinant is irreducible and anti-invariant under the Galois involution τ\tau.

Since the last two coordinates are preserved by φ\varphi, we have

τ⁡(z)=z,τ⁡(w)=w.\tau(z)=z,\qquad\tau(w)=w.

We compute the Jacobian determinant:

|J⁡(φ)|=2​w2​x−z2.\left|J(\varphi)\right|=2w^{2}x-z^{2}.

By Theorem 4.3.3,

τ⁡(2​w2​x−z2)=2​w2​τ​(x)−z2=−(2​w2​x−z2),\tau(2w^{2}x-z^{2})=2w^{2}\,\tau(x)-z^{2}=-(2w^{2}x-z^{2}),

hence

τ⁡(x)=−x+z2w2.\tau(x)=-x+\frac{z^{2}}{w^{2}}.

Since f2=z​x+w​yf_{2}=zx+wy is invariant under τ\tau, we obtain

z​τ​(x)+w​τ​(y)=z​x+w​y.z\,\tau(x)+w\,\tau(y)=zx+wy.

Substituting the expression for τ⁡(x)\tau(x) gives

−z​x+z3w2+w​τ​(y)=z​x+w​y,-zx+\frac{z^{3}}{w^{2}}+w\,\tau(y)=zx+wy,

and therefore

τ⁡(y)=y+2​zw​x−z3w3.\tau(y)=y+\frac{2z}{w}x-\frac{z^{3}}{w^{3}}.

Thus the Galois involution is given by

τ⁡(x,y,z,w)=(−x+z2w2,y+2​zw​x−z3w3,z,w).\tau(x,y,z,w)=\left(-x+\frac{z^{2}}{w^{2}},\;y+\frac{2z}{w}x-\frac{z^{3}}{w^{3}},\;z,\;w\right).
